title: Backyard Basketball Court Cost
metaDescription: What a backyard basketball court costs in Canada: tile kit prices by size from a 25 x 20 ft half court to a full court, plus the pad and hoop you source.
h1: How much does a backyard basketball court cost in Canada?
intro: The total has three parts: the tile kit, the concrete or asphalt pad under it, and the hoop. Here is what each one involves and what the kits cost by size.
answer: A backyard basketball court in Canada has three costs: the tile kit, the pad and the hoop. Half court tile kits run from $3,420 for 25 x 20 ft to $9,970 for 50 x 30 ft, before freight and tax. The concrete or asphalt pad and the hoop are sourced locally, so get quotes for both.

sections.h2: The three parts of the budget
paragraphs: A tile court is a surface, not a whole project. The kit covers the tiles for the full footprint, edge pieces, game lines and a numbered layout plan. It sits on a flat, hard base that you build or already own, and you add the hoop of your choice.
That means three separate numbers. The kit price is fixed by size and listed below. The pad and the hoop depend on your yard, your region and your taste, so they are priced locally.

sections.h2: Half court kit prices by size
paragraphs: A half court is the size to look at first if the court has to fit beside a garage or at the back of a suburban lot. Prices are for the tile kit, before freight and tax.

rows: A square pad with a full free-throw line

paragraphs: A full court needs length as well as budget. The compact 65 x 35 ft kit keeps two hoops and a centre line in a large backyard. The 84 x 50 ft kit matches a high school court and the 94 x 50 ft kit is regulation length.

The base is the part of the budget we cannot price for you. Concrete is the best base and asphalt works well. What a pad costs depends on site access, how much grading the yard needs, local material prices and the season. Ask two or three local contractors to quote the exact footprint of the kit you are considering.

If you already have a firm, reasonably level driveway, patio slab or old court, you may not need a new pad at all. Tiles can go over an existing hard surface, which removes the largest unknown from the budget. Check with your local municipality before pouring anything new, since rules on lot coverage and setbacks vary.
The hoop is not part of the kit. An in-ground hoop is set in its own footing, and a portable hoop rolls onto the finished court. Pick the one that suits your players and price it separately.

Kits ship on pallets by freight carrier, and freight depends on your postal code and the size of the kit. Request a quote and we reply with a delivered price and a layout drawing. Sales tax is added based on your province. Tiles snap together by hand with a rubber mallet, so there is no labour to hire for the surface.

faqs.q: How much does a half court basketball court cost?
faqs.a: Tile kits for a half court range from $3,420 for a 25 x 20 ft pad to $9,970 for a 50 x 30 ft pad, before freight and tax. The classic 30 x 25 ft size is $5,160. Add the cost of the pad and a hoop, both sourced locally.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to build a basketball court on an existing driveway?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. If the driveway or slab is firm and reasonably level, tiles can go straight over it and you skip the cost of a new pad. Low spots and heaves should be levelled first.

faqs.q: How much does a full size backyard basketball court cost?
faqs.a: Full court tile kits start at $14,470 for a compact 65 x 35 ft court. A high school size 84 x 50 ft kit is $26,090 and a regulation 94 x 50 ft kit is $29,330, all before freight and tax.

title: Backyard Pickleball Court Cost
metaDescription: What a backyard pickleball court costs in Canada: tile kit prices for compact, recommended and multi-sport sizes, plus the pad and net you source separately.
h1: How much does a backyard pickleball court cost in Canada?
intro: Two pickleball kits and two multi-sport kits cover the backyard sizes. Here is what each one costs and what else belongs in the budget.
answer: A backyard pickleball court tile kit costs $9,600 for a compact 52 x 28 ft pad or $11,670 for the recommended 60 x 30 ft pad, before freight and tax. The concrete or asphalt base, the net and any fencing or lighting are separate costs, so get local quotes for the pad.

paragraphs: A pickleball court is 20 ft wide and 44 ft long. The surface around those lines is what turns a set of lines into a playable court, and it is most of what you are buying. A kit covers tiles for the whole pad, edge pieces, the court lines with the kitchen in its own colour and a numbered layout plan.
The base under the tiles, the net and posts, fencing and lighting are not in the kit. Budget for them separately.
Prices are for the tile kit only, before freight and tax.

paragraphs: Both pickleball kits carry the same full-size 20 x 44 ft lines, with a 7 ft kitchen on each side of the net. The difference is run-off. The 60 x 30 ft pad leaves 8 ft behind each baseline and 5 ft beside each sideline. The 52 x 28 ft pad leaves 4 ft on every side.

If the yard and the budget allow it, the larger pad plays better because you can move back for a deep lob. If the court has to share the yard with a pool or a patio, the compact pad keeps the lines regulation and gives up some room around them.

sections.h2: Adding basketball to the same pad
paragraphs: The 60 x 30 ft multi-sport kit is the same price as the 60 x 30 ft pickleball kit, $11,670, and adds a basketball key and arc at one end in a second line colour. The 50 x 30 ft multi-sport kit is $9,890 and fits both games on a shorter pad.
The added cost of the second sport is mostly the hoop, which you choose and buy separately.

sections.h2: The pad, the net and freight
paragraphs: Concrete is the best base and asphalt works well. Pad pricing depends on your site and your region, so ask local contractors to quote the exact footprint. An existing slab or an old court can be reused if it is firm and reasonably level, which takes the largest unknown out of the budget.
For the net, a portable system rolls on and off, and surface-mount posts are the more permanent option. Regulation height is 36 in at the posts and 34 in at the centre.
Kits ship by freight on pallets, and we quote a delivered price to your postal code. Check with your local municipality before pouring a new pad or adding fencing or lights.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to build a pickleball court in your backyard?
faqs.a: The tile kit is $9,600 for a 52 x 28 ft court or $11,670 for a 60 x 30 ft court, before freight and tax. The pad underneath, the net and any fencing or lighting are extra and are priced locally.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to build a backyard pickleball court?
faqs.a: Reuse a hard surface you already have. If an existing slab, driveway or old court is firm, level and large enough, tiles can go over it and the pad cost disappears. Laying the tiles yourself avoids labour for the surface.

faqs.q: Is a multi-sport court more expensive than a pickleball court?
faqs.a: Not for the tiles. The 60 x 30 ft multi-sport kit and the 60 x 30 ft pickleball kit are both $11,670 before freight and tax. You add the cost of a hoop.

title: Backyard Court Size Guide
metaDescription: Backyard court size guide for Canada: see which basketball, pickleball, multi-sport, tennis and shuffleboard court kits fit the space you have, in feet.
h1: Backyard court size guide: what fits in your yard
intro: Start with the flat space you have, then match it to a sport. Every size below is the pad footprint in feet.
answer: A basketball half court fits on a pad as small as 25 x 20 ft. A full pickleball court needs at least 52 x 28 ft, and 60 x 30 ft is the recommended size. A pad 50 x 30 ft or larger can hold both games. Shuffleboard fits a strip 6 ft wide and 42 to 52 ft long.

paragraphs: Measure the flat, usable rectangle, not the whole yard. Leave out slopes, tree roots, drainage swales and anything a ball should not hit, like a window or a neighbour's fence. Write down the width and the depth in feet.
Courts sit on a concrete or asphalt pad, so the pad size is the court size. Check with your local municipality about setbacks and lot coverage before you settle on a footprint.

sections.h2: What fits in the space you have
paragraphs: Find the row closest to your flat area. If you are between two rows, the smaller kit fits and can be sized up.

head: Flat space available
What fits
Kit size
rows: Half court with room at the top of the arc
Full-width half court, or basketball plus pickleball
Recommended pickleball, or multi-sport with a hoop

paragraphs: Width decides how much of the three-point arc you get. Depth decides how far back you can shoot. A 25 x 20 ft pad fits the key, with the free-throw line near the back edge. At 25 ft deep there is standing room behind the free-throw line. At 30 ft deep you can shoot from the top of the arc, and at 50 ft wide you have the full width of a regulation court.
Full courts start at 65 x 35 ft. A high school court is 84 x 50 ft and a regulation court is 94 x 50 ft.
The playing lines are always 20 x 44 ft. The recommended total is 30 x 60 ft, which the 60 x 30 ft kit matches. The compact 52 x 28 ft kit keeps the same lines with less run-off.
A pad 30 ft wide and 50 to 60 ft long holds a pickleball court down the middle and a basketball half court at one end, each in its own line colour.
A doubles tennis court is 78 x 36 ft, and the standard total footprint is 60 x 120 ft. The recreational kit trims that to 110 x 50 ft.
Shuffleboard goes the other way. A regulation court is 52 x 6 ft, so it fits along a fence line or beside a pool where no other court would. A double court with two lanes is 52 x 16 ft.

sections.h2: If your pad is an odd size
paragraphs: Tiles are roughly one foot square, so any kit can be resized in about 1 ft steps in either direction. The listed sizes are starting points. If the court will sit against a wall, a curb or a fence, allow for a small expansion gap around the perimeter.

faqs.q: What is a good size for a backyard basketball court?
faqs.a: For a half court, 30 x 25 ft fits a full key, a free-throw line and a good part of the three-point arc. A 25 x 20 ft pad works for tighter yards and younger players. Go to 30 ft deep if you want to shoot from the top of the arc.

faqs.q: What is the minimum size for a backyard pickleball court?
faqs.a: The lines are 20 x 44 ft. A 52 x 28 ft pad is a practical minimum, with 4 ft of run-off on every side. The recommended total is 30 x 60 ft.

faqs.q: Can one backyard court fit both basketball and pickleball?
faqs.a: Yes. A pad 30 ft wide and at least 50 ft long fits a full pickleball court and a basketball half court at one end, with each game in its own line colour.

title: Court Tiles vs Concrete vs Asphalt
metaDescription: Modular court tiles vs painted concrete vs asphalt for a backyard court in Canada. Compare drainage, heat, joint impact, ball bounce, upkeep and repair.
h1: Court tiles vs painted concrete vs asphalt: which surface for a home court?
intro: All three can be played on. They differ in how they handle water, heat, hard landings and Canadian winters.
answer: Modular court tiles sit on top of a concrete or asphalt pad, so the choice is really about the playing surface. Tiles drain through, have some give underfoot and can be repaired one piece at a time. Painted or coated concrete gives the liveliest bounce but shows cracks. Bare asphalt is simplest but runs hot and rough.

paragraphs: Every home court starts with a hard base. Bare asphalt is that base left as it is. Painted or acrylic-coated concrete is a slab with a colour coating and lines applied on top. A tile court is the same slab or asphalt with an interlocking tile surface laid over it.
So tiles do not replace the pad. They change what you play on, and they can go over a pad you already own.
The comparison below is general. Any surface is only as good as the base under it.

head: Factor
Modular tile
Coated concrete
Bare asphalt
rows: Open grid lets water through to the pad
Water sits until it runs off or dries
Dark surface runs hot in full sun
Good when new, less even as it wears
Recoat and repaint lines over time

paragraphs: An open-grid tile lets rain and meltwater pass through to the pad below, where it runs off along the slope of the base. The playing surface sits above the water, so the court is usable sooner after a shower.
On coated concrete and asphalt, water stays on the surface until it drains or evaporates, and low spots hold puddles.
Dark asphalt absorbs sun and can be uncomfortable on a hot afternoon. Tiles stay cooler than bare asphalt, and lighter colours help further.

Tiles also have a little give, so the surface is slightly softer than bare concrete under running and jumping feet. Concrete and asphalt have none. Bare asphalt is also the roughest of the three on knees and elbows.

Coated concrete gives the liveliest bounce. Sport tiles give a consistent bounce on a flat base. It is slightly lower than on painted concrete, and recreational players adjust to it quickly. Asphalt bounces well when new and less evenly as it weathers.

sections.h2: Maintenance and repair through Canadian winters
paragraphs: Freeze-thaw cycles open hairline cracks in most slabs over time. On a coated court those cracks come through the coating and the lines, and the fix is patching and recoating. Tiles float on top of the pad, so small cracks underneath do not show on the playing surface. If a tile is damaged, it can be unsnapped and replaced.
Tiles do need a small expansion gap at the perimeter and a base that is flat. Heaves and low spots in the pad should be fixed before any surface goes down.
The trade-off is cost. A tile surface is an extra purchase on top of the pad, while bare concrete or asphalt needs nothing more to start playing.

faqs.q: Are court tiles better than concrete for a backyard basketball court?
faqs.a: Tiles go on top of concrete, so you get both. Compared with playing on the bare or painted slab, tiles drain faster, have more give underfoot and hide the hairline cracks slabs develop. Painted concrete has a slightly livelier bounce.

faqs.q: Can you put sport tiles over asphalt?
faqs.a: Yes. Asphalt is a fine base as long as it is firm and reasonably flat. Low spots and heaves should be levelled first. Tiles can also go over an old asphalt driveway or tennis court.

faqs.q: Do court tiles get hot in the sun?
faqs.a: Any outdoor surface warms up in direct sun. Tiles stay cooler than bare asphalt, and lighter tile colours stay cooler than dark ones.

faqs.q: Do you still need a concrete pad under court tiles?
faqs.a: Yes. Tiles need a flat, hard base. Concrete is best and asphalt works well. They are not made to sit on grass, soil or loose gravel.

title: Basketball Court Dimensions
metaDescription: Basketball court dimensions in feet: NBA and high school court sizes, key width, free-throw line, rim height and three-point distances for a backyard in Canada.
h1: Basketball court dimensions, from regulation to backyard half court
intro: The official numbers, and how they scale down to fit a pad beside the garage.
answer: An NBA court is 94 ft long and 50 ft wide. A high school court is 84 ft by 50 ft. The rim is 10 ft high and the free-throw line is 15 ft from the backboard. The key is 12 ft wide in high school and 16 ft in the NBA.

paragraphs: Two full-court sizes are the usual reference points. Both are 50 ft wide. They differ in length and in the lines inside.

head: Measurement
High school
NBA
rows: 23 ft 9 in, 22 ft in the corners

sections.h2: The key, the free-throw line and the rim
paragraphs: The rim is 10 ft above the playing surface at every level. The free-throw line is 15 ft from the face of the backboard. The backboard hangs 4 ft in from the baseline, so the free-throw line sits 19 ft from the baseline.

The key, also called the lane or the paint, is the rectangle between the baseline and the free-throw line. It is 12 ft wide on a high school court and 16 ft wide in the NBA. Our backyard kits are planned around the 12 ft key.

Three-point distance is measured from the centre of the basket. The high school line is 19 ft 9 in. The NBA line is 23 ft 9 in at the top and 22 ft in the corners, where the line runs straight and parallel to the sideline.
Because the basket sits a little over 5 ft in from the baseline, the top of a high school arc lands about 25 ft from the baseline. An NBA arc reaches about 29 ft.

sections.h2: Scaling down to a backyard half court
paragraphs: A regulation half court is 42 to 47 ft deep and 50 ft wide, which is more than many yards can spare. The lines that matter for shooting practice are all close to the hoop, so a much smaller pad still plays properly.
list: 20 ft deep: the key and the free-throw line fit, with the line near the back edge of the pad.
25 ft deep: standing room behind the free-throw line, and the top of a high school arc right at the back edge.
30 ft deep: room to shoot from behind the top of a high school arc.
30 to 35 ft wide: the key and both wings. A full-distance high school arc is about 40 ft across, so at these widths the arc is drawn to suit the pad.
45 to 50 ft wide: room for a full-distance high school arc, corners included.

sections.h2: Choosing lines for a home court
paragraphs: Decide who the court is for. Younger players get more from a full key and a clear free-throw line than from a distant arc. Older players who want game-distance threes need 30 ft of depth and as much width as the yard allows.

Tiles are roughly one foot square, so a kit can be resized in about 1 ft steps to match your pad. The layout drawing shows where every line lands before anything is produced. It assumes a standard 4 ft backboard overhang unless you tell us otherwise.

faqs.q: How big is a half court basketball court?
faqs.a: A regulation half court is 50 ft wide and 42 ft deep for high school or 47 ft deep for the NBA. Backyard half courts are smaller. Kits run from 25 x 20 ft up to 50 x 30 ft.

faqs.q: How far is the free-throw line from the hoop?
faqs.a: The free-throw line is 15 ft from the face of the backboard, which puts it 19 ft from the baseline.

faqs.q: How far is the three-point line in high school and the NBA?
faqs.a: The high school three-point line is 19 ft 9 in from the centre of the basket. The NBA line is 23 ft 9 in at the top of the arc and 22 ft in the corners.

faqs.q: How high is a basketball hoop?
faqs.a: The rim is 10 ft above the court at every level from high school to the NBA. Many adjustable hoops can be lowered for younger players.

title: Winter Care for Court Tiles
metaDescription: Winter care for outdoor court tiles in Canada: leave the tiles down, clear snow with a plastic shovel or blower, skip rock salt and plan a spring clean-up.
h1: Winter care for outdoor court tiles in Canada
intro: The court stays where it is. A few habits in fall, winter and spring keep it ready for the first warm day.
answer: Outdoor court tiles stay down all winter in Canada. Clear snow with a plastic shovel, a broom or a blower. Avoid rock salt, metal blades and ice chippers. Keep the expansion gap at the perimeter clear of soil and stones, then sweep and rinse the court in spring before the first game.

sections.h2: Leave the tiles where they are
paragraphs: There is no need to lift a tile court for winter. The tiles are made to stay outdoors year-round, and the open-grid surface lets meltwater drain through to the pad instead of pooling on top.
What does come inside is the equipment. Roll a portable pickleball net into the garage, and follow the hoop maker's advice for storing a portable hoop.
A clean court going into winter is an easier court in spring.
list: Blow or sweep off leaves, seeds and twigs so they do not sit wet in the grid all winter.
Rinse off mud and anything sticky with a garden hose.
Walk the perimeter and check that the expansion gap is clear of soil, mulch and stones.
Store nets, balls and loose equipment.
Mark the court edges with driveway stakes if you plan to clear snow.

paragraphs: You do not have to clear the court. Snow can sit on the tiles all winter. If you want to play on a mild day, clear it gently.

Use a plastic shovel, a stiff broom or a leaf blower for light snow. A snow blower is fine if the scraper bar and skid shoes are raised so no metal touches the tiles. Push along the surface instead of chopping down into it.

sections.h2: What to keep off the court
paragraphs: Ice on a tile court is best left to the sun. Meltwater drains through the grid as it goes.
list: Rock salt. It leaves residue in the grid and is hard on the concrete underneath.
Metal shovels, steel plow blades and ice chippers, which can gouge the tile surface.
Sand and grit, which pack into the grid and have to be washed out in spring.

paragraphs: Tiles expand in heat and contract in cold, like any plastic surface. A Canadian yard can swing from deep cold in January to a hot pad in July, so the court needs room to move. That is the reason for the small gap between the edge of the court and any wall, curb, post or fence.

If the gap fills with soil, or the court is pinned tight against something solid, the surface has nowhere to go when it expands. Keep the perimeter free so the court can move as the temperature changes.
Once the snow is gone, blow or sweep off whatever winter left behind. Then rinse the court with a garden hose so grit washes through the grid and off the pad.
Check the edges. If a tile has lifted at a seam, press it down and tap it home with a rubber mallet. Put the net back up, check the hoop hardware, and play.

faqs.q: Can you leave court tiles outside in winter?
faqs.a: Yes. Outdoor court tiles are made to stay down year-round, including through Canadian winters. Leave a small expansion gap at the perimeter and keep it clear.

faqs.q: Can you shovel snow off court tiles?
faqs.a: Yes, with a plastic shovel, a broom or a blower. Avoid metal blades and ice chippers, which can gouge the surface.

faqs.q: Can you use salt on outdoor court tiles?
faqs.a: Skip rock salt. It leaves residue in the grid and is hard on the concrete pad underneath. Clear loose snow and let the sun melt the rest.
